a: as Moses' custom requires
t: Circumcised, and living by Moses' custom
p: Codex Bezae makes the demand broader: circumcision and a whole way of life under the law.

readings.w: Nearly all manuscripts, including Sinaiticus (01), Vaticanus (03) and the Byzantine text; SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House GNT, Textus Receptus (KJV)
readings.en: you are circumcised by the custom of Moses
readings.plain: as Moses' custom requires

readings.w: Codex Bezae (05, about 400) with a Syriac margin reading and a Coptic witness (as reported by Metzger)
readings.orig: περιτμηθῆτε καὶ τῷ ἔθει Μωϋσέως περιπατῆτε
readings.en: you are circumcised and walk by the custom of Moses
readings.plain: and live as Moses' custom requires

why: The shorter text has overwhelming support. Bezae's wording looks like an explanation, spelling out that the visitors wanted Gentile believers to keep the whole law (as 15:5 says), which is typical of the Western text of Acts.
b: The Western text of Acts, best known from Codex Bezae, is about eight or nine percent longer than the text in most modern Bibles, and chapter 15 shows it at work again in 15:2, 20, 29 and 34.

a: So they arranged for Paul and Barnabas and some others from their group to go up to Jerusalem, to the apostles and elders, about this dispute.
t: Paul insists, and the men from Jerusalem give orders
p: Codex Bezae expands the verse: Paul argues that converts should stay as they were, and the Judeans send him to be judged.

readings.w: Nearly all manuscripts; SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House GNT, Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV)
readings.orig: ἔταξαν ἀναβαίνειν Παῦλον καὶ Βαρναβᾶν καί τινας ἄλλους ἐξ αὐτῶν πρὸς τοὺς ἀποστόλους καὶ πρεσβυτέρους εἰς Ἰερουσαλὴμ περὶ τοῦ ζητήματος τούτου
readings.en: they appointed Paul and Barnabas and some others of them to go up to the apostles and elders at Jerusalem about this question
readings.plain: So they arranged for Paul and Barnabas and some others from their group to go up to Jerusalem, to the apostles and elders, about this dispute.

readings.w: Codex Bezae (05), partly supported by Syriac and other versions (as reported by Metzger)
readings.orig: ἔλεγεν γὰρ ὁ Παῦλος μένειν οὕτως καθὼς ἐπίστευσαν διισχυριζόμενος· οἱ δὲ ἐληλυθότες ἀπὸ Ἰερουσαλὴμ παρήγγειλαν αὐτοῖς τῷ Παύλῳ καὶ Βαρναβᾷ καί τισιν ἄλλοις ἀναβαίνειν ... ὅπως κριθῶσιν ἐπ’ αὐτοῖς
readings.en: for Paul spoke, firmly insisting that they remain as they were when they believed; but those who had come from Jerusalem ordered them, Paul and Barnabas and some others, to go up ... so that they might be judged before them
readings.plain: For Paul kept insisting that they should stay just as they were when they came to believe. But the men who had come from Jerusalem ordered Paul and Barnabas and some others to go up to Jerusalem, to the apostles and elders, to be judged before them about this dispute.

why: The longer form is found almost only in Bezae and its allies and has the marks of a later retelling: it makes Paul's position explicit and puts the Jerusalem visitors in charge of Antioch. Editors keep the text of the great majority of manuscripts. The Greek of the second reading is given in part (the dots mark words shared with the first).

a: God made his choice among you
t: "Among you" or "among us"
p: The critical editions have Peter say God chose "among you." The Byzantine text and the KJV have "among us."

readings.w: The older manuscripts; SBLGNT, NA27/NA28, Tyndale House GNT
readings.en: among you God chose
readings.plain: God made his choice among you

readings.w: Later manuscripts; Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV "God made choice among us")
readings.en: God chose among us
readings.plain: God made his choice among us

why: In Greek "you" (hymin) and "us" (hēmin) differed by one letter and sounded alike in later pronunciation, so copyists often confused them. "Among you" is the better-attested reading and fits Peter addressing the council; "among us" makes Peter include himself. The sense hardly changes: God chose, from the group of apostles and elders, that Peter should preach to the Gentiles.

a: The whole gathering went quiet.
t: Did the elders agree with Peter?
p: Codex Bezae and a few other witnesses add that the elders agreed with what Peter had said.

readings.w: Nearly all manuscripts; SBLGNT, NA27/NA28, Tyndale House GNT, Byzantine text, Textus Receptus
readings.en: and all the multitude fell silent
readings.plain: The whole gathering went quiet.

readings.w: Bezae (05, about 400) and a few other witnesses (as reported by Metzger)
readings.orig: συγκατατεθεμένων δὲ τῶν πρεσβυτέρων τοῖς ὑπὸ τοῦ Πέτρου εἰρημένοις ἐσίγησεν πᾶν τὸ πλῆθος
readings.en: and when the elders had agreed to what had been said by Peter, all the multitude fell silent
readings.plain: The elders agreed with what Peter had said, and the whole gathering went quiet.

why: A typical Western expansion: it spells out what the silence implies and gives the elders a formal part in the decision. It has too little support to be original.

a: things known from ages past.
t: "Known from long ago" or "Known to God are all his works"
p: The oldest manuscripts end the quotation with two words. Later ones make it a full sentence, as in the KJV.

readings.w: Sinaiticus (01), Vaticanus (03), Ephraemi (04) and others; SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House GNT
readings.en: known from of old
readings.plain: things known from ages past.

readings.w: Later manuscripts, with several different longer forms (Alexandrinus and Bezae have one of them, as reported by Metzger); Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV "Known unto God are all his works from the beginning of the world")
readings.orig: γνωστὰ ἀπ’ αἰῶνός ἐστιν τῷ θεῷ πάντα τὰ ἔργα αὐτοῦ
readings.en: known from of old to God are all his works
readings.plain: Known to God from ages past are all his works.

why: The short reading is in the oldest witnesses and is the harder one: the two words hang loosely after the quotation, and copyists completed them in more than one way to make a sentence. The longer text turns an echo of Isaiah 45:21 into a statement about God's foreknowledge. The two words can also be joined to 15:17: "the Lord, who makes these things known from long ago" (the punctuation of NA28).

a: from sexual sin, from what is strangled and from blood
t: Three food rules and a moral law
p: The decree has four items in most manuscripts. Bezae makes it three moral rules plus the Golden Rule; P45 has three food rules.

readings.w: Sinaiticus (01), Vaticanus (03), Alexandrinus (02), the Byzantine text; SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House GNT, Textus Receptus (KJV)
readings.orig: καὶ τῆς πορνείας καὶ τοῦ πνικτοῦ καὶ τοῦ αἵματος
readings.en: and from sexual immorality and from what is strangled and from blood
readings.plain: from sexual sin, from what is strangled and from blood

readings.w: Codex Bezae (05) and Irenaeus in Latin, with some other witnesses (as reported by Metzger)
readings.orig: καὶ τῆς πορνείας καὶ τοῦ αἵματος καὶ ὅσα μὴ θέλουσιν ἑαυτοῖς γίνεσθαι ἑτέροις μὴ ποιεῖν
readings.en: and from sexual immorality and from blood, and not to do to others whatever they do not want done to themselves
readings.plain: from sexual sin and from blood, and not to do to others what they would not want done to themselves

readings.w: Papyrus 45 (about 250) and the Ethiopic version (as reported by Metzger)
readings.orig: καὶ τοῦ πνικτοῦ καὶ τοῦ αἵματος
readings.en: and from what is strangled and from blood
readings.plain: from what is strangled and from blood

why: The four-item text is far better attested and explains the others. Without "strangled," the remaining items, idolatry, sexual sin and blood, can be read as the three great sins of idolatry, adultery and murder, and the Golden Rule, in its negative form found in Tobit 4:15 and the Didache, makes the moral reading complete. That looks like a later reinterpretation from a time when the food rules no longer made sense to Gentile churches. P45's omission of sexual sin turns the list into food laws only, probably for the same kind of reason.
b: See the note on 15:20 for what the four rules were for, and 15:29 for the same variants in the letter.

a: who are brothers
t: "Brothers" or "and the brothers"
p: The oldest text calls the apostles and elders themselves brothers. Later copies add the whole church as senders.

readings.w: The oldest manuscripts, including Sinaiticus (01), Alexandrinus (02) and Vaticanus (03) (as reported by Metzger); SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House GNT
readings.orig: οἱ ἀπόστολοι καὶ οἱ πρεσβύτεροι ἀδελφοί
readings.en: the apostles and the elders, brothers
readings.plain: who are brothers

readings.w: Later manuscripts; Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV "The apostles and elders and brethren")
readings.orig: οἱ ἀπόστολοι καὶ οἱ πρεσβύτεροι καὶ οἱ ἀδελφοί
readings.en: the apostles and the elders and the brothers
readings.plain: and the brothers

why: The older witnesses lack "and the." Copyists probably added it to match 15:22, where the whole church joins the decision, or because "the elders, brothers" seemed awkward. With the shorter text the apostles and elders write as brothers to brothers.

a: thrown your souls into turmoil
t: "Saying you must be circumcised and keep the law"
p: The Byzantine text and the KJV spell out what the troublemakers said.

readings.w: The oldest manuscripts, including Sinaiticus (01), Alexandrinus (02) and Vaticanus (03) (as reported by Metzger); SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House GNT
readings.en: unsettling your souls
readings.plain: thrown your souls into turmoil

readings.w: Later manuscripts (Metzger lists Ephraemi, 04, among them); Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV "saying, Ye must be circumcised, and keep the law")
readings.orig: ἀνασκευάζοντες τὰς ψυχὰς ὑμῶν, λέγοντες περιτέμνεσθαι καὶ τηρεῖν τὸν νόμον
readings.en: unsettling your souls, saying you must be circumcised and keep the law
readings.plain: thrown your souls into turmoil, saying you must be circumcised and keep the law

why: The added words repeat 15:1 and 15:5 and look like an explanatory note that entered the text. The oldest manuscripts do not have them. The meaning is the same either way.

a: from blood, from what is strangled and from sexual sin. If you keep yourselves clear of these, you will be doing well.
t: The decree in the letter: four items or three, and the Golden Rule
p: As in 15:20, Bezae drops "what is strangled" and adds the Golden Rule, and ends with "carried along by the Holy Spirit."

readings.w: Sinaiticus (01), Vaticanus (03), Alexandrinus (02), the Byzantine text; SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House GNT, Textus Receptus (KJV)
readings.orig: καὶ αἵματος καὶ πνικτῶν καὶ πορνείας· ἐξ ὧν διατηροῦντες ἑαυτοὺς εὖ πράξετε
readings.en: and from blood and from things strangled and from sexual immorality; if you keep yourselves from these, you will do well
readings.plain: from blood, from what is strangled and from sexual sin. If you keep yourselves clear of these, you will be doing well.

readings.w: Codex Bezae (05) and Irenaeus in Latin; Tertullian also knows the decree without "strangled" (as reported by Metzger)
readings.orig: καὶ αἵματος καὶ πορνείας, καὶ ὅσα μὴ θέλετε ἑαυτοῖς γίνεσθαι ἑτέρῳ μὴ ποιεῖν· ἀφ’ ὧν διατηροῦντες ἑαυτοὺς εὖ πράξατε φερόμενοι ἐν τῷ ἁγίῳ πνεύματι
readings.en: and from blood and from sexual immorality, and whatever you do not want done to yourselves, do not do to another; if you keep yourselves from these, you will do well, being carried along by the Holy Spirit
readings.plain: from blood and from sexual sin, and do not do to anyone else what you would not want done to yourselves. If you keep yourselves clear of these, you will be doing well, carried along by the Holy Spirit.

why: The reasons are those given at 15:20: the four-item decree is the better-attested and older form, and the moral version reflects a later church for which rules about meat no longer made sense.

a: back to those who had sent them
t: "Those who had sent them" or "the apostles"
p: The Byzantine text and the KJV say Judas and Silas returned "to the apostles."

readings.w: The oldest manuscripts, including Sinaiticus (01), Alexandrinus (02) and Vaticanus (03); SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House GNT
readings.en: to those who had sent them
readings.plain: back to those who had sent them

readings.w: Later manuscripts; Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV "unto the apostles")
readings.en: to the apostles
readings.plain: back to the apostles

why: The oldest witnesses have "those who had sent them"; the shorter "the apostles" names the senders, perhaps by a copyist's simplification (the two words look alike in Greek). The meaning is nearly the same, since the apostles and elders had sent them.

a: [The oldest manuscripts do not have this verse.]
t: Did Silas stay in Antioch?
p: Verse 34, "But Silas decided to remain there," is a later addition that explains how Silas could be at Antioch in 15:40.

readings.w: Sinaiticus (01), Alexandrinus (02), Vaticanus (03), most later manuscripts; SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House GNT, Robinson-Pierpont Byzantine text
readings.en: (no verse 34)
readings.plain: [The oldest manuscripts do not have this verse.]

readings.w: Ephraemi (04, 400s), Bezae (05, about 400), minuscules 33, 614, 1739 and others, some Old Latin manuscripts; Textus Receptus (KJV "Notwithstanding it pleased Silas to abide there still"). Bezae adds "and Judas went alone" (as reported by Metzger)
readings.orig: ἔδοξεν δὲ τῷ Σίλᾳ ἐπιμεῖναι αὐτοῦ
readings.en: but it seemed good to Silas to remain there
readings.plain: But Silas decided to remain there.

why: The verse is missing from the oldest manuscripts and from most Byzantine ones. It was evidently added to solve a puzzle: 15:33 says Judas and Silas went back to Jerusalem, yet in 15:40 Paul chooses Silas at Antioch. The added verse, which contradicts 15:33, keeps Silas in Antioch. Without it, Silas may simply have come back later, or Paul sent for him. The verse came into the Textus Receptus and the KJV from manuscripts like those listed and from the Latin.
b: The site keeps the KJV numbering, so this line marks the verse's place. Its Greek here is the Textus Receptus form, since the Robinson-Pierpont Byzantine text does not have it.

a: Barnabas wanted to bring
t: "Wanted" or "determined"
p: The critical text says Barnabas "wanted" to take Mark. The Byzantine text and the KJV say he "determined" to.

readings.w: The older manuscripts; SBLGNT, NA27/NA28, Tyndale House GNT
readings.en: was wanting
readings.plain: Barnabas wanted to bring

readings.w: Later manuscripts; Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV "Barnabas determined to take with them John")
readings.en: resolved, decided
readings.plain: Barnabas made up his mind to bring

why: The two verbs differ by a few letters. The critical text's imperfect suggests a wish Barnabas kept pressing; the Byzantine aorist makes it a settled decision. Either way Paul refused, and the quarrel followed. The Byzantine text also lacks the "as well" (kai) before John's name.

a: the Lord's grace
t: The grace "of the Lord" or "of God"
p: The oldest copies say the brothers entrusted Paul to the Lord's grace. The Byzantine text and the KJV say God's grace.

readings.w: The oldest manuscripts, including Sinaiticus (01), Alexandrinus (02) and Vaticanus (03); SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House GNT
readings.en: to the grace of the Lord
readings.plain: the Lord's grace

readings.w: Later manuscripts; Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV "the grace of God")
readings.en: to the grace of God
readings.plain: God's grace

why: The older witnesses read "the Lord." "God" probably came in from 14:26, where Paul and Barnabas had been "handed over to God's grace" at the start of the first journey.

a: They crossed the Phrygian and Galatian country, and the Holy Spirit kept them from speaking the word in Asia.
t: "They crossed" or "when they had gone through"
p: The critical text makes the crossing a main verb. The Byzantine text and the KJV make it a participle: "Now when they had gone throughout Phrygia."

readings.w: The older manuscripts; SBLGNT, NA27/NA28, Tyndale House GNT
readings.orig: Διῆλθον δὲ τὴν Φρυγίαν καὶ Γαλατικὴν χώραν, κωλυθέντες
readings.en: they went through the Phrygian and Galatian region, having been prevented
readings.plain: They crossed the Phrygian and Galatian country, and the Holy Spirit kept them from speaking the word in Asia.

readings.w: Later manuscripts; Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV "Now when they had gone throughout Phrygia and the region of Galatia, and were forbidden")
readings.orig: Διελθόντες δὲ τὴν Φρυγίαν καὶ τὴν Γαλατικὴν χώραν, κωλυθέντες
readings.en: having gone through Phrygia and the Galatian region, having been prevented
readings.plain: They went through Phrygia and the Galatian country, having been kept by the Holy Spirit from speaking the word in Asia.

why: The Byzantine form smooths the sentence into a chain of participles running into 16:7, and its extra "the" before "Galatian" lets "Phrygia" stand as a separate region. The difference matters to the debate over which Galatia Paul visited (see the note "Which Galatia?"): in the critical text the barring from Asia may come before the crossing, while the Byzantine chain sets the two side by side.

a: the Spirit of Jesus
t: "The Spirit of Jesus" or "the Spirit"
p: The oldest manuscripts have the unusual phrase "the Spirit of Jesus." Later ones, and the KJV, say only "the Spirit."

readings.w: P74, Sinaiticus (01), Alexandrinus (02), Vaticanus (03), Bezae (05) and the early versions; SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House GNT
readings.en: the Spirit of Jesus
readings.plain: the Spirit of Jesus

readings.w: Later manuscripts; Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV "the Spirit suffered them not"); a few manuscripts read "the Spirit of the Lord" or "the Holy Spirit"
readings.en: the Spirit
readings.plain: the Spirit

why: "The Spirit of Jesus" occurs nowhere else in the New Testament, and its strangeness explains why copyists changed it to familiar forms or dropped "of Jesus." Metzger notes it is supported by early and widespread witnesses. The phrase matters for theology: the Holy Spirit of 16:6 is called the Spirit of the risen Jesus (compare Romans 8:9; Philippians 1:19).

a: God had summoned us
t: Called by God or by the Lord
p: The oldest manuscripts say God had called them. The Byzantine text and the KJV say "the Lord."

readings.w: The oldest manuscripts, including Sinaiticus (01), Alexandrinus (02) and Vaticanus (03); SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House GNT
readings.en: God
readings.plain: God had summoned us

readings.w: Bezae (05) and later manuscripts; Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV "the Lord had called us")
readings.en: the Lord
readings.plain: the Lord had summoned us

why: The older and wider witness is to "God." Changes between "God" and "the Lord" are among the commonest small variants in Acts and do not change the sense.

a: one of the foremost cities of its district of Macedonia
t: "A leading city" or "a city of the first district"
p: The manuscripts read "a first city of the district." A few editions adopt a reading that makes it "a city of the first district."

readings.w: Sinaiticus (01), Alexandrinus (02) and most manuscripts (Vaticanus with a small difference); SBLGNT, Tyndale House GNT
readings.en: a first city of the district of Macedonia
readings.plain: one of the foremost cities of its district of Macedonia

readings.w: NA27 and NA28 (whose text of Acts is the same) and UBS4/UBS5, adopting "first" in the genitive (πρώτης), a reading found in some Latin and medieval versions but in no Greek manuscript (as reported by Metzger)
readings.en: a city of the first district of Macedonia
readings.plain: a city of the first district of Macedonia

readings.w: Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV "the chief city of that part of Macedonia")
readings.orig: πρώτη τῆς μερίδος τῆς Μακεδονίας πόλις
readings.en: the first city of the district of Macedonia
readings.plain: the foremost city of its district of Macedonia

why: The Romans divided Macedonia into four districts, and Philippi lay in the first. Since Amphipolis, not Philippi, was the capital of that district, the reading "first city" seemed wrong to some editors, who chose "a city of the first district" with very slight support; Metzger reports that the committee was divided. But prōtē without the article can mean "a leading city," a title Greek cities claimed for themselves, so the reading of the manuscripts makes good sense. The Plain follows the manuscripts with the SBL and Tyndale House editions. (Some electronic edition data mark NA28 with the manuscript reading here; that is a data error, since NA28 did not change the text of Acts.)

a: walked out of the gate to a river. We expected to find a place of prayer there.
t: "Where we supposed there was a place of prayer" or "where prayer was usually made"
p: The editions read "gate" and "we supposed there was a place of prayer." The Byzantine text and the KJV read "city" and "it was thought" (KJV "where prayer was wont to be made").

readings.w: The older manuscripts in various forms; NA27 and NA28 (the same text of Acts), SBLGNT, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort
readings.orig: ἔξω τῆς πύλης παρὰ ποταμὸν οὗ ἐνομίζομεν προσευχὴν εἶναι
readings.en: outside the gate by a river, where we supposed there was a place of prayer
readings.plain: walked out of the gate to a river. We expected to find a place of prayer there.

readings.w: Later manuscripts; Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV "out of the city by a river side, where prayer was wont to be made")
readings.orig: ἔξω τῆς πόλεως παρὰ ποταμόν, οὗ ἐνομίζετο προσευχὴ εἶναι
readings.en: outside the city by a river, where a place of prayer was thought to be (or, as the KJV takes it, where prayer was customarily made)
readings.plain: walked out of the city to a river, where there was thought to be a place of prayer.

why: The Greek of this verse is tangled in the manuscripts, and Metzger treats it as badly confused. "Gate" is the harder and better-supported word: "city" is the easier, general term. "We supposed" fits travelers who did not know the town. The Byzantine enomizeto can mean "was thought to be," or, as the KJV took it, "was customarily" ("where prayer was wont to be made"). Either way, there was a Jewish place of prayer by the river. (Some electronic edition data mark NA28 with the Byzantine wording; NA28 did not change the text of Acts and reads as NA27.)

a: They are telling you a way to be saved!
t: "To you" or "to us"
p: The slave girl says Paul's party tells "you" the way. The Byzantine text and the KJV have "us."

readings.w: The majority of the older manuscripts; SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House GNT
readings.en: they proclaim to you a way of salvation
readings.plain: They are telling you a way to be saved!

readings.w: Some manuscripts; Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV "which shew unto us the way of salvation")
readings.en: they proclaim to us a way of salvation
readings.plain: They are telling us a way to be saved!

why: In Greek "you" (hymin) and "us" (hēmin) sounded alike when the manuscripts were copied, so they are often confused. "To you," addressed to the bystanders, suits the cry of someone advertising the preachers. The KJV also has "the way," but no Greek manuscript has the article.

a: the Lord Jesus
t: "The Lord Jesus" or "the Lord Jesus Christ"
p: The oldest manuscripts have "the Lord Jesus." The Byzantine text and the KJV add "Christ."

readings.w: The oldest manuscripts, including Sinaiticus (01) and Vaticanus (03); SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House GNT
readings.en: the Lord Jesus
readings.plain: the Lord Jesus

readings.w: Later manuscripts and some older ones; Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV "the Lord Jesus Christ")
readings.en: the Lord Jesus Christ
readings.plain: the Lord Jesus Christ

why: Copyists tended to fill out the names of Jesus, especially in solemn formulas. The shorter form is older.

a: They came and appealed to them. Then they led them out and kept asking them to go away from the city.
t: The magistrates apologize at length
p: Codex Bezae expands the scene: the magistrates come with friends, admit they were wrong, and fear another riot.

readings.w: Nearly all manuscripts; SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House GNT, Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV)
readings.orig: καὶ ἐλθόντες παρεκάλεσαν αὐτούς, καὶ ἐξαγαγόντες ἠρώτων ἀπελθεῖν ἀπὸ τῆς πόλεως
readings.en: and they came and appealed to them, and they brought them out and asked them to leave the city
readings.plain: They came and appealed to them. Then they led them out and kept asking them to go away from the city.

readings.w: Codex Bezae (05) and some allies (as reported by Metzger)
readings.en: they came with many friends to the prison and urged them to leave, saying, 'We did not know the truth about you, that you are righteous men'; and they brought them out and urged them, saying, 'Leave this city, so that they do not gather against you again, shouting against you'
readings.plain: They came to the prison with many friends and appealed to them. "We did not know the truth about you," they said, "that you are righteous men." Then they led them out and appealed to them: "Leave this city, so that they do not gather again and shout against you."

why: Bezae's lively additions in this chapter (also at 16:30 and 16:35, where the magistrates remember the earthquake) are typical of the Western text's fondness for filling in motives and speeches. They are not found in the older Alexandrian witnesses or the Byzantine text. The Greek of Bezae's long form is not given here; the English follows Metzger's summary.

a: many women of the first rank
t: Leading women, or wives of leading men
p: Codex Bezae reads "wives of the leading men," making the women's standing depend on their husbands.

readings.w: Nearly all manuscripts; SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House GNT, Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV "of the chief women not a few")
readings.orig: γυναικῶν τε τῶν πρώτων οὐκ ὀλίγαι
readings.en: and of the leading women not a few
readings.plain: many women of the first rank

readings.w: Codex Bezae (05) (as reported by Metzger)
readings.orig: καὶ γυναῖκες τῶν πρώτων οὐκ ὀλίγαι
readings.en: and not a few wives of the leading men
readings.plain: many wives of the leading men

why: The difference is small in Greek but changes the picture. Ben Witherington has argued that several readings of the Western text in Acts lower the standing of women (here, 17:12 and 17:34), so Bezae's form is better explained as a later change than the other way around.

a: The Jews, though, burned with jealousy.
t: "The Jews" or "the Jews who did not believe"
p: The Byzantine text and the KJV say it was "the Jews which believed not" who were moved with envy.

readings.w: The oldest manuscripts, including Sinaiticus (01), Alexandrinus (02) and Vaticanus (03); SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House GNT
readings.en: but the Jews, becoming jealous
readings.plain: The Jews, though, burned with jealousy.

readings.w: Later manuscripts (Bezae with a different order); Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV "But the Jews which believed not, moved with envy")
readings.en: but the disobedient Jews, becoming jealous
readings.plain: The Jews who did not believe, though, burned with jealousy.

why: The shorter reading is in the oldest witnesses. The addition makes clear what the context already shows, that some Jews had believed (17:4). It is a fair interpretation, and the Plain's note on 17:5 makes the same point.

a: and so did a good number of Greeks, prominent women and men alike.
t: Women first, or men first
p: Codex Bezae rearranges the verse so that the men come first and the women are not called prominent.

readings.w: Nearly all manuscripts; SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House GNT, Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV)
readings.orig: καὶ τῶν Ἑλληνίδων γυναικῶν τῶν εὐσχημόνων καὶ ἀνδρῶν οὐκ ὀλίγοι
readings.en: and of the Greek women of high standing and of men, not a few
readings.plain: and so did a good number of Greeks, prominent women and men alike.

readings.w: Codex Bezae (05) (as reported by Metzger)
readings.orig: καὶ τῶν Ἑλλήνων καὶ τῶν εὐσχημόνων ἄνδρες καὶ γυναῖκες ἱκανοί
readings.en: and of the Greeks and of those of high standing, men and women, a considerable number
readings.plain: and so did a good number of Greeks and people of standing, men and women.

why: Bezae's change of order fits the pattern noted at 17:4 and 17:34. The usual text puts the respected Greek women first.

a: shaking up the crowds and throwing them into confusion.
t: "And throwing them into confusion"
p: The Byzantine text and the KJV lack the second verb: "stirred up the people."

readings.w: The older manuscripts; SBLGNT, NA27/NA28, Tyndale House GNT
readings.en: shaking and troubling the crowds
readings.plain: shaking up the crowds and throwing them into confusion.

readings.w: Later manuscripts; Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV "stirred up the people")
readings.en: shaking the crowds
readings.plain: shaking up the crowds.

why: The second verb repeats the word used of the riot at Thessalonica (17:8, "threw the crowd ... into alarm"), so it ties the two scenes together. It may have dropped out as redundant, or been added to match 17:8; the editions keep it on the strength of the older manuscripts.

a: to make his way to the coast
t: To the sea, or "as it were to the sea"
p: The Byzantine text and the KJV say Paul went "as it were to the sea," as if heading for the coast to throw off pursuers.

readings.w: The oldest manuscripts, including Sinaiticus (01), Alexandrinus (02) and Vaticanus (03); SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House GNT
readings.en: to go as far as to the sea
readings.plain: to make his way to the coast

readings.w: Later manuscripts; Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV "to go as it were to the sea")
readings.en: to go as if to the sea
readings.plain: to make his way as if to the coast

why: The older reading heōs, "as far as," says simply that the brothers escorted Paul to the coast, where he took ship for Athens. Hōs, "as if," may be a copyist's slip (the words differ by one letter in Greek), and it gave rise to the idea of a feint, with Paul in fact going to Athens by land.

a: what you revere without knowing it, that is what I announce to you
t: "What" or "whom" you worship
p: The oldest text says "what" and "this" in the neuter. The KJV's "Whom ye ignorantly worship, him" follows later manuscripts.

readings.w: The oldest manuscripts, including Sinaiticus (01), Alexandrinus (02) and Vaticanus (03); SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House GNT
readings.en: what therefore you revere without knowing, this
readings.plain: what you revere without knowing it, that is what I announce to you

readings.w: Later manuscripts; Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV "Whom therefore ye ignorantly worship, him declare I unto you")
readings.en: whom therefore you revere without knowing, him
readings.plain: the one you revere without knowing him, he is the one I announce to you

why: The neuter is the older and harder reading: Paul does not say the Athenians already worship the true God as a person. He speaks of "what" they reverence without knowing, the divine as they dimly sensed it, and then names the true God. Copyists made it personal, "whom" and "him."

a: out of one person
t: "From one" or "of one blood"
p: The oldest manuscripts say only "from one." The KJV's "of one blood" follows later manuscripts.

readings.w: The oldest manuscripts, including Sinaiticus (01), Alexandrinus (02) and Vaticanus (03); SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House GNT
readings.en: from one
readings.plain: out of one person

readings.w: Bezae (05), later manuscripts and Irenaeus (as reported by Metzger); Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV "hath made of one blood all nations of men")
readings.en: from one blood
readings.plain: out of one blood

why: "Blood" is probably an explanatory addition: it tells the reader what "one" means. Without it, "one" most naturally means one man, Adam. The KJV's "of one blood" became famous in the American struggles over slavery and civil rights, quoted as proof of the unity of the human race; the shorter text says the same thing.

a: look for God
t: Seek God, or seek the Lord
p: The oldest manuscripts say "God." The Byzantine text and the KJV say "the Lord."

readings.w: Sinaiticus (01), Alexandrinus (02), Vaticanus (03); SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House GNT
readings.en: to seek God
readings.plain: look for God

readings.w: Later manuscripts; Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV "That they should seek the Lord")
readings.en: to seek the Lord
readings.plain: look for the Lord

why: "God" fits a speech to pagans, where Paul avoids the biblical title "the Lord." The change to "the Lord" echoes the familiar Old Testament call to seek the LORD (Isaiah 55:6).

a: Dionysius the Areopagite, a woman called Damaris,
t: Is Damaris named?
p: Codex Bezae leaves Damaris out and calls Dionysius "an Areopagite of high standing."

readings.w: Nearly all manuscripts; SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House GNT, Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV)
readings.orig: Διονύσιος ὁ Ἀρεοπαγίτης καὶ γυνὴ ὀνόματι Δάμαρις
readings.en: Dionysius the Areopagite and a woman named Damaris
readings.plain: Dionysius the Areopagite, a woman called Damaris,

readings.w: Codex Bezae (05) (as reported by Metzger)
readings.en: a certain Dionysius, an Areopagite of high standing
readings.plain: a certain Dionysius, an Areopagite of high standing,

why: Bezae's text drops the woman and gives her honorific, "of high standing," to Dionysius. All other witnesses name Damaris. The change fits the Western text's pattern of lowering the place of women in Acts (see 17:4 and 17:12).
